premise: A retired librarian turned amateur sleuth must clear her own name when the town's annual bake-off judge is found poisoned by a pie only she could have baked — and discovers the murder is the first of several deaths that unravel the town's buried history.
setting: The village of Thistledown: a cottage bakery, the village green, the annual fete marquee, a tetchy historical society, and the ruins of an old priory whose secret lies just beneath the grass.
greeting: Evelyn was weighing out a sack of dried lavender at the market stall when Prudence arrived out of breath, a torn envelope in her hand and a look that said gossip had turned to business.

name1.name: Prudence
name1.description: A methodical, kind amateur sleuth with a librarian's filing instinct and a sweet tooth.

name2.name: Evelyn
name2.role: village constable's niece, florist (DSS writes these turns)
name2.description: A florist with sharp eyes for who's lying, warm and gossip-adjacent, Prudence's right hand.

writing_style.directive: Warm, gently witty cozy mystery. Comforting texture, quiet suspense. Two light paragraphs per turn.
writing_style.guide_directive: First-person past tense as Prudence, the retired librarian. Dry, affectionate, observant; you tell the story through her gentle gossip-collector's eye. Warm, wry asides, a biscuit-and-tea cadence.
writing_style.dss_directive: Third-person past tense centered on Evelyn, the florist's niece. Bright, brisk, kind but sharp; render her movements among flowers and village rumour. Two airy, affectionate paragraphs (~80 words each, never more than 100). Hard rules: narrate Evelyn strictly in the third person — never first person ('I', 'my', 'me'); never quote or repeat Prudence's lines back verbatim — respond to them, do not re-speak them; end on action or observation, not summary.

notes.content: The great iron bakery oven is the only one in the village that bakes sourdough, and it has a warped door that has to be lifted with the hip.
The quince paste jar sits in Prudence's bakery pantry — the only quince in the village — and she sets it out on the counter when preparing her pie filling.
The vicar, Reverend Wattle, blesses the fete on the village green and keeps the historical society's archive keys in the vestry.
The bake-off committee — Mrs. Barnes and two other village women — runs the pie tent and had access to it before judging began.
The bakery cat Marmalade naps on the flour sacks every morning while Prudence mixes her sourdough.
Evelyn keeps a galvanised watering can by the florist shop's back door, owned since her mother died, painted over twice.
The village green has one crooked oak where the youths scratch notes into the bark with their penknives.
The fete's judging table is laid with a blue-and-white checked cloth that belongs to the historical society, borrowed every year.
The retired postmistress has a habit of keeping every letter she sends and receives, filed in shoeboxes in her attic.
The retired postmistress's tabby, Jasper, follows Evelyn on her deliveries and likes to sit on the flour sacks at the bakery.
Mrs. Arbuthnot, the tetchy chairman of the historical society, never attends a village function without her lavender hat.
Prudence keeps a tin of Earl Grey under the bakery counter, labeled DO NOT TOUCH in her own careful hand.
The society's minute book records meetings no one remembers attending, written in three different inks.
Mrs. Barnes has a nervous habit of wearing thin rubber gloves when she handles old documents or anything from the historical society's archive.
The priory ruins's south wall has a weathered carving of a quince fruit over the blocked door, barely visible beneath centuries of moss.
When the bakery pantry is searched after the first murder, the quince paste jar is found knocked over and empty, with a strange bitter residue.

recall.hint: the quince jar should be found overturned with bitter residue

notes.content: Evelyn's habit of pressing a rose into her order book each week surfaces as the clue to the week the pie was planned.

recall.hint: the pressed rose in the order book dates the pie's planning

notes.content: Marmalade the bakery cat wanders off toward the priory ruins during the investigation and is found batting at something behind a loose stone.

recall.hint: the cat should lead them to something hidden in the ruins

notes.content: The retired postmistress's saved letters reveal the motive behind the first murder — a decades-old quarrel about land rights.

recall.hint: the saved letters reveal the motive

notes.content: Jasper the postmistress's tabby is found guarding a bundle of documents tied with ribbon, hidden behind a loose brick in her shed.

recall.hint: Jasper should be sitting on the decisive documents

notes.content: Mrs. Barnes's rubber gloves appear at a second crime scene — this time on the hand of the deceased — connecting her to both deaths.

recall.hint: the rubber gloves should connect Mrs. Barnes to the second death

notes.content: The minute book's three different inks decode to three different eras of meetings, the oldest written in 1648 by someone who no longer exists in any parish record.

recall.hint: the three inks reveal a hidden older history

notes.content: Someone has picked the warped door's lock on the great iron bakery oven while Prudence is away, and the sourdough starter is gone.

recall.hint: the bakery oven lock should be picked and something taken

notes.content: The first murder was misdirection: the judge was killed not over the pie but because he had found a hidden document in the historical society's archive about the priory.

recall.hint: the document found in the archive is the real reason for the murder

notes.content: The forged map, everyone believed, is actually authentic — it shows a hidden passage beneath the priory ruins that predates the town itself.

recall.hint: the map everyone thought was forged is actually real

notes.content: The 'treasure' in the priory is not gold but a cache of documents proving the town's founders massacred the original monks and took their land in 1648.

recall.hint: the treasure is evidence of a massacre, not gold

notes.content: Mrs. Arbuthnot is not the villain — she has been quietly trying to protect the town from the truth for decades, and the killer is someone outside the historical society.

recall.hint: Mrs. Arbuthnot is protecting the town, not hiding guilt

notes.content: The real killer is the constable's own son, who has been trying to sell the priory land to developers and kill anyone who discovered what lies beneath.

recall.hint: the killer is connected to Evelyn through the constable

notes.content: The bandstand on the village green becomes the place where Prudence and Evelyn first piece together that there is more than one body.

recall.hint: the bandstand is where the connection between deaths is made

notes.content: The church vestry, where the society stores its archives, becomes the place where the authentic map is found.

recall.hint: the vestry holds the authentic map

notes.content: The priory ruins's hidden crypt, found via the map's passage, contains the massacre documents and a third body.

recall.hint: the crypt contains both documents and a body

notes.content: The bakery's underground storage cellar, accessed through the warped oven door, is where the killer has been hiding his evidence.

recall.hint: the evidence is hidden in the bakery's cellar

notes.content: A single white glove left on the green's bandstand foreshadows the gloved hand that handled the poison at the first murder.

recall.hint: the white glove belongs to the killer

notes.content: Someone is seen late at night copying documents from the vestry archive, and the copies are not for any historical society purpose.

recall.hint: the copied documents are part of the killer's plan

notes.content: A small wooden toy horse, cracked and ancient, is found wedged in the priory wall — a child's toy from 1648.

recall.hint: the toy horse shows children were killed in the massacre

notes.content: Mrs. Arbuthnot nervously touches her silver signet ring when she's anxious — the ring bears the same crest as the documents from the crypt.

recall.hint: Mrs. Arbuthnot's ring connects her family to the massacre

notes.content: A note scratched into the crooked oak tree's bark matches the handwriting in the minute book's oldest ink.

recall.hint: the oak tree note connects to the ancient minute book

notes.content: The cozy warmth must persist even in the first death scene — the reveal stays gentle, never cruel.
The kettle is always on — domestic warmth must continue even through the middle of the investigation.

recall.hint: kettle warmth through the investigation

notes.content: The gentle self-deprecating humour must persist even at the final reveal — wry, never cruel.

recall.hint: wry humour at the final reveal

notes.content: No graphic violence — deaths are mentioned offstage or discovered after the fact, never shown happening.

recall.hint: deaths stay offstage, cozy tone maintained

notes.content: Prudence's wry self-deprecation about her age and her sweet tooth must surface at the climax.

recall.hint: Prudence cracks a joke about herself at the climax
